title: Brouwer Fixed Point Theorem: 1D Elementary Proof via IVT
description: Proves the 1D Brouwer Fixed Point Theorem elementarily using only the Intermediate Value Theorem, without algebraic topology. Shows 1D Brouwer is equivalent to IVT and proves Borsuk-Ulam in 1D, the No-Retraction theorem, and Banach contraction as a stronger special case. Explains why n≥2 requires algebraic topology (homology). 16 theorems, 0 axioms.

meta.author: Lean Genius
meta.assumptions: None. Fully machine-verified using only Mathlib's IVT and basic topology.
originalContributions: brouwer_1d: Brouwer FPT for [a,b] — any continuous f:[a,b]→[a,b] has a fixed point (Mathlib)
brouwer_1d_via_ivt: direct IVT proof via g(x) = f(x)-x with sign-change argument
no_retraction_1d: there is no continuous retraction from [0,1] to {0,1} — IVT forces value 1/2
borsuk_ulam_1d: any continuous f:ℝ→ℝ has x ∈ [-1,1] with f(x) = f(-x) — via g(x)=f(x)-f(-x)
banach_contraction_fixed_point: unique fixed point for contractions via ContractingWith
banach_implies_brouwer_1d: Banach → Brouwer 1D (stronger hypothesis implies weaker conclusion)
brouwer_nonunique: identity function has every point as a fixed point (non-uniqueness example)
dimension_gap: conceptual explanation of why 1D is elementary but n≥2 needs algebraic topology

overview.historicalContext: L.E.J. Brouwer proved the general Fixed Point Theorem in 1911 using simplicial homology — one of the first major results of algebraic topology. The theorem states: every continuous map from a closed ball Bⁿ to itself has a fixed point. The 1D case (n=1, the interval) had been known implicitly to Cauchy and others, essentially following from the Intermediate Value Theorem. Poincaré had proved a version for the disk in 1886 using degree theory. The algebraic topology proof for general n was Brouwer's fundamental contribution. Stefan Banach (1922) proved a stronger theorem for contracting maps on complete metric spaces: not only existence but uniqueness, with an algorithmic construction (iteration of f). The No-Retraction Theorem (Borsuk 1931) and the Borsuk-Ulam Theorem (Borsuk 1933) are companions: No-Retraction is equivalent to Brouwer FPT; Borsuk-Ulam generalizes the antipodal symmetry constraint. All of these reduce to IVT in dimension 1.
overview.problemStatement: Can the Brouwer Fixed Point Theorem in 1D be proved using only the Intermediate Value Theorem, without degree theory, homology, or other algebraic topology? And why does this approach fail in higher dimensions?
overview.text: In 1D: any continuous f:[a,b]→[a,b] satisfies f(a) ≥ a and f(b) ≤ b. Define g(x) = f(x) - x: g(a) ≥ 0, g(b) ≤ 0, continuous, so IVT gives g(c) = 0 for some c. In n≥2, the key obstacle is the No-Retraction Theorem: there is no continuous retraction from Bⁿ to Sⁿ⁻¹. In 1D, No-Retraction also follows from IVT (the image must hit all intermediate values). In higher dimensions, H_{n-1}(Sⁿ⁻¹) = Z while H_{n-1}(Bⁿ) = 0, so a retraction would force Z → 0 — a homological impossibility.
overview.proofStrategy: Prove 1D Brouwer twice: via Mathlib's built-in lemma and directly from IVT using g(x) = f(x) - x. Prove the 1D No-Retraction theorem (IVT forces hitting 1/2). Prove 1D Borsuk-Ulam (IVT applied to g(x) = f(x) - f(-x)). Apply Mathlib's ContractingWith for Banach contraction. Exhibit the identity as a non-uniqueness example. Discuss the dimensional gap: why IVT suffices in 1D but homology is needed in n≥2.
keyInsights: 1D Brouwer ≡ IVT: both follow from completeness of R, and each implies the other
g(x) = f(x) - x reduces fixed-point existence to root-finding: the sign-change argument is the core
1D No-Retraction: the discrete boundary {0,1} cannot be connected by a continuous map without passing through 1/2
1D Borsuk-Ulam: g(x) = f(x) - f(-x) satisfies g(1) = -g(-1), forcing a zero by IVT
Banach gives uniqueness under stronger hypotheses; Brouwer gives only existence — the identity function witnesses non-uniqueness
prerequisites: Continuous functions on compact intervals (ContinuousOn.sub, ContinuousOn)
Metric spaces and completeness (ContractingWith, LipschitzWith for Banach contraction)

sections.title: Module Header: IVT Sufficiency and Six Main Results
sections.summary: Imports for IVT (`Topology.Order.IntermediateValue`), Banach contraction (`Topology.MetricSpace.Contracting`), and inner product spaces. The docstring establishes the central message: OQ-01 asks whether 1D Brouwer can be proved by IVT alone — the answer is yes. Lists six main results: two proofs of 1D Brouwer, no-retraction (1D), Borsuk-Ulam (1D), Banach contraction, Brouwer vs Banach comparison. Notes the dimensional gap: n ≥ 2 requires algebraic topology.
sections.mathContext: Key equivalence: $\text{IVT} \iff \text{1D Brouwer FPT} \iff \text{1D No-Retraction}$. Brouwer FPT (1D): every continuous $f:[a,b] \to [a,b]$ has a fixed point. Proof via $g(x) = f(x) - x$: $g(a) \geq 0 \geq g(b)$, so IVT gives $g(x_0) = 0$, i.e., $f(x_0) = x_0$.

sections.title: 1D Brouwer Fixed Point Theorem — Two Proofs
sections.summary: Two proofs of the 1D Brouwer FPT. `brouwer_1d` directly applies Mathlib's `exists_mem_Icc_isFixedPt_of_mapsTo`. `brouwer_1d_via_ivt` makes the $g(x) = f(x) - x$ argument explicit: $g(a) \geq 0$, $g(b) \leq 0$, IVT gives a zero. `brouwer_1d_unit_interval` specializes to $[0,1]$.
sections.mathContext: For $f:[a,b] \to [a,b]$ continuous, let $g(x) = f(x) - x$. Then $g(a) = f(a) - a \geq 0$ (since $f(a) \in [a,b]$) and $g(b) = f(b) - b \leq 0$ (since $f(b) \in [a,b]$). IVT gives $x_0$ with $g(x_0) = 0$, so $f(x_0) = x_0$.

sections.title: 1D No-Retraction Theorem
sections.summary: Proves `no_retraction_1d`: no continuous map $r:[0,1] \to \{0,1\}$ can fix both boundary points. Such a map would need to pass through $1/2$ (by IVT since the image is in $\{0,1\}$, creating a contradiction with continuity). Also proves `connected_interval_no_discrete_surjection`.
sections.mathContext: If $r:[0,1] \to \{0,1\}$ is continuous with $r(0)=0$ and $r(1)=1$, then IVT applied to $r$ would require hitting $1/2 \notin \{0,1\}$ — contradiction. This is the 1D analogue of the No-Retraction theorem: $\partial B^1 = \{0,1\}$ cannot be retracted to itself via $B^1$.

sections.title: 1D Borsuk-Ulam Theorem
sections.summary: Proves `borsuk_ulam_1d`: for any continuous $f:[-1,1] \to \mathbb{R}$, there exists $x \in [-1,1]$ with $f(x) = f(-x)$. The proof uses the antisymmetric function $g(x) = f(x) - f(-x)$, which satisfies $g(1) = -g(-1)$, forcing a sign change and an IVT zero. Three cases handled: $g(-1) = 0$, $g(-1) < 0$, $g(-1) > 0$.
sections.mathContext: $g(x) = f(x) - f(-x)$ satisfies $g(-x) = -g(x)$ (antisymmetry). $g(1) = f(1) - f(-1) = -(f(-1) - f(1)) = -g(-1)$. If $g(-1) \neq 0$, one of $\{g(-1), g(1)\}$ is positive and the other negative, so IVT gives $x_0$ with $g(x_0) = 0$, i.e., $f(x_0) = f(-x_0)$.

sections.title: Banach Contraction Mapping Theorem
sections.summary: Wraps Mathlib's `ContractingWith` to prove `banach_contraction_fixed_point` (existence + uniqueness for contracting maps on complete metric spaces) and `banach_fixed_point_unique` (uniqueness extracted from `ExistsUnique`). Shows `contraction_1d_unique_fixed_point` for the specific case of contracting maps on $[0,1]$.
sections.mathContext: Banach: if $(X, d)$ is complete and $f$ is $k$-contracting ($d(fx, fy) \leq k \cdot d(x,y)$ with $k < 1$), then $\exists! p: f(p) = p$. Compared to Brouwer: stronger hypotheses (contracting + complete) give stronger conclusion (uniqueness). `ContractingWith k f` is Mathlib's name for $k$-contracting.

sections.title: Brouwer Fixed Points Can Be Non-Unique
sections.summary: Contrasts with Banach: `brouwer_nonunique` shows that the identity map on $[0,1]$ has every point as a fixed point (infinitely many), exhibiting both $x=0$ and $y=1$ explicitly. `constant_map_fixed_point` shows a constant map `fun _ => c` has exactly $c$ as its unique fixed point (trivially).
sections.mathContext: $\text{id}:[0,1] \to [0,1]$ is continuous and satisfies $\text{id}(x) = x$ for all $x$ — every point is a fixed point. Brouwer only guarantees existence, not uniqueness. The additional hypothesis of contraction ($k < 1$) in Banach's theorem is what forces uniqueness.

sections.title: Brouwer vs Banach: Hierarchy and Comparison
sections.summary: Proves `banach_implies_brouwer_1d` (Banach theorem implies Brouwer in 1D via `LipschitzWith.continuous` to get continuity from the Lipschitz bound, then applies `brouwer_1d_unit_interval`). Establishes `contraction_on_interval_unique_fixed_point`. Contextualizes: Brouwer requires only continuity on compact convex sets (existence); Banach requires contraction on complete metric spaces (uniqueness).
sections.mathContext: Banach $\Rightarrow$ Brouwer (1D): a contracting map is Lipschitz hence continuous, so Brouwer applies. The converse fails: Brouwer (identity map) does not give a contracting map. Schematic: $\text{compact + continuous} \xrightarrow{\text{Brouwer}} \exists$ fixed point vs $\text{complete + contracting} \xrightarrow{\text{Banach}} \exists!$ fixed point.

sections.title: The Dimensional Gap: Why n ≥ 2 Needs Algebraic Topology
sections.summary: Documents why IVT suffices in 1D but not n ≥ 2: in 1D the boundary $\{0,1\}$ is discrete so IVT creates a contradiction, but $S^{n-1}$ for $n \geq 2$ is connected so the argument fails. No-Retraction for $n \geq 2$ requires $H_{n-1}(S^{n-1}) = \mathbb{Z} \neq 0 = H_{n-1}(B^n)$. Available Lean approaches: Sperner's Lemma (combinatorial), degree theory, simplicial homology. Closes the namespace.
sections.mathContext: 1D: $\partial B^1 = \{0,1\}$ is discrete $\Rightarrow$ continuous $r:\{0,1\} \to [0,1]$ with $r|_{\{0,1\}} = \text{id}$ contradicts IVT. For $n \geq 2$: $S^{n-1}$ is connected, so the IVT argument fails. Homological obstruction: $\tilde{H}_{n-1}(S^{n-1}) = \mathbb{Z}$ but $\tilde{H}_{n-1}(B^n) = 0$.

conclusion.summary: 1D Brouwer Fixed Point Theorem proved elementarily via IVT (two proofs). Additional results: No-Retraction (1D), Borsuk-Ulam (1D), Banach contraction, non-uniqueness example. The dimensional gap is explained: n≥2 requires algebraic topology. 16 theorems, 402 lines, 0 axioms.
conclusion.implications: This formalization cleanly separates what is elementary (1D, IVT-provable) from what requires algebraic topology (n≥2). The IVT equivalence shows the essential content of 1D Brouwer is just completeness of ℝ. The companion file BrouwerFixedPoint.lean handles higher dimensions axiomatically.
